title: Who are some filmmakers that have a strong sense of theme and symbolism in their filmography?

commenti.body:
>I find myself having to apply death of the author in order to get at any theme in their stories which then makes me feel like I’m reading something into their works that’s just not there.

That's the thing, something that the author intended "isn't there" either.

It's only there if you find it as a member of the audience - meaning is generated by the audience. 

So don't worry too much about what the filmmaker (or author) says, worry more about your own experience and what you feel might be the experience others have. Keep in mind that those others are incredibly diverse (time , race, sex, class, education, whether or not they're the target audience, etc.). 

As for which films to watch, I don't really have a particular suggestion because I feel that any of the critically-acclaimed films out there have strong themes. Symbolism is a tough one, it's such a misused phrase in everyday criticism so I'm not sure what you mean by it. 

Maybe you could suggest some interesting themes you like to see expressed in film and we could go off that?

I like the theme of ‘ignorance deters the attainment of bliss’ in Kaufman’s Eternal Sunshine or ‘humans are an end in themself, not a means to an end’ in Fury Road. Or what I believe the theme of Leviathan by Zvyagintsev ‘quietism(resignation) is a reasonable response in the face of a corrupt sovereign power’. I’m  honestly only recently getting into more artful films, whereas I have always loved literature. So I’m a bit new to taking in the more artful films that are not meant as pure entertainment but to make you think.

I think Bong Jun Ho and Park Chan Wook 

Despite doing great with storytelling , delivering a great narrative and being masters of directing, with their framing, blocking and staging. Their movies would have been great on their own but the attention to detail and how they are ladden with so many symbols elevate them to works of art. Thus adding to your experience even after multiple viewing.

It sounds like you might not understand “death of the author” … it’s a postmodern extension of “intentional fallacy” which means precisely there ISN’T anything in the text that the author could possibly imbue. All that there is is the text, and the reader is free to recontextualize meaning in the way that they interact with the text. If you think that meaning of Blood Meridian is that Albino people are evil well Cormac McCarthy might disagree with you, but CM was also just combining various motifs, themes, and literary traditions and there’s no little homuncular Cormac in that book that if you find him then he’ll tell you what it’s about. And by that extension, McCarthy probably WOULD agree with that, as he’s pretty existentialist to me, so he would agree that the world is meaningless but we are driven by a need for meaning. 

And I would say that the film makers you listed are great BECAUSE their symbols are nebulous and not some hamfisted 19th century Miss Havisham.

Not sure, how you got that I misunderstood what death of the author is. It’s a pretty simple concept and your definition of it is compatible with my definition. Also, I don’t think a theme being not nebulous is the same as hamfisted. I just think it shows that the creator knew what they were communicating.

That’s the thing … you can’t “communicate” meaning, at least according to those that employ death of the author. The fissures, lacunae, ruptures, and deconstructions that are inherent in “text” as difference make it impossible. You can arrange a text so that it resonates meaning with the author in a particular way, but there is no way to actually “saturate” the text with a concrete meaning.

Now I think you misunderstand death of the author. The idea isn’t that there can be no communication of meaning, but that the text not the author, communicates the meaning through an interplay with audience who understands it subjectively.  This idea that there can be no inherent meaning to a text that is not explicit endears itself to a belief that one can have no ability for inference. Looking at Banshees of Inishirin I find it funny when people completely miss what’s in it. That there is meaning behind the symbols that are static and not prone to deconstruction, as you say. It is not a matter of whether there is a static meaning in the work, but a matter of whether one has the ability to cognitively extrapolate through pattern recognition what those meanings are.

Also it seems like you deleted your response that I was responding to and have also made a lengthy edit after I responded but I typed up another response so I’m just gonna post it:

Speaking as a fan of Barthes, Derrida, et al, I would say the only thing that Ulysses as a text “means” is a book that starts “Stately plump Buck Mulligan” and ends with “yes yes yes” The only thing that Seventh Seal “means” is 90 or so minutes of celluloid film projected at 24 frames per second. That is the communication, that is the “text” as gramma, print, message literally as a letter, possibly wax-sealed by the author’s signet ring. Saying “you think it’s funny that people miss what’s in Banshees” is exactly the point — there’s nothing IN there at all! It’s just captured light. However, our minds phenomenologically cannot but think meaningfully. Symbols have historical nature which allows us to arrange them in a way that we can try and express a sentiment … a woman in blue holding a dead son is going to be VERY evocative to a good chunk of people, but that is not because this is some INHERENTLY Marianne image … perhaps right now people in Palestine would interpret it wildly different. Or perhaps someone hates their mother and wishes the roles were divorced. “Symbolism” according to the most proponents of DotA accrue “meaning” not from anything inherent but from historical play of difference. Passion Plays and Horacio Alger stories can be read as an interesting look into a temporal time completely removed from any intrinsic meaning, but at their time they were read and deeply understood by many to express some true meaning. Also “cognitively extrapolate” is another term that DotA practitioners would have a big problem with. There is nothing to extrapolate. Again, that assumes an inherent meaning or quaila than can be unearthed which is precisely the opposite of Death of the Author.

Villeneuve has pretty heavy symbolism - I'm thinking of Enemy and Prisoners, although even the really mainstream stuff like Dune and Blade Runner lean into it. The bullfighter stuff in Dune especially has a lot to dig into if you're familiar with the book.

I will always lean towards authorial intent over death of the author. In the same way that an axiom derived from science can only be 99 percent true as opposed to 100 percent true, there is still evidence to support it being a justified true belief epistemically which can be applied to a text. So to can we say from evidence present in text that there is a meaning to be derived inherent within it. We may not be able to say with a hundred percent certainty whether Banshees of Inishirin is an allegory for the Irish civil war, but we can say based on evidence that there is a stronger case that is than it is not and that we do so by seeing the evidence for what it is as a justified true belief. To say that Banshees of Inishirin is about what cats believe about Stalin, has no basis in evidence but under the view of death of the author would be equally as valid as the belief that the story is an allegory for the Irish civil war. One is a justified true belief, and the other is not. 

Personally, I’m not a fan of Barthes. His theory lends itself to nihilism more than existentialism. It’s not that there is no meaning to communicate, it is just that it is the author who imbues meaning whereas if we place the meaning as purely coming from the reader’s interpretation we reach a place where meaning has well, lost all meaning. Meaning from a linguistically semantic sense must be static. If say the word grass can mean anything in the whole dictionary as opposed to the specific static definition of vegetation consisting of typically short plants with long, narrow leaves, growing wild then the word has lost all meaning. Ultimately, applying the same logic, death of the author loses all meaning by placing meaning as any and everything a reader might conjecture thus losing meaning itself since meaning to some degree must be static. Thus Barthes and death of the author is ultimately nihilistic, not existential as many proponents would have us believe.

This has turned into an argument of “Death of the Author” itself based on your very misunderstanding of it as opposed to your expressed attempt to see cinema through that lens so it’s probably not appropriate for this forum. But suffice to say I don’t think you understand it, nor do you understand Nihilism and Existentialism, and by extension the structuralist and post-structuralist framework upon which a lot of that rests wherein meaning is PRECISELY from the derivation of meaning from the movement of meaning as opposed to something inherent.
